title: Module 1: Quality Control
text: remove four categories genes, specific reasons: 1. Nuclear-encoded mitochondrial genes (~200 genes) genes nuclear genome encode proteins functioning within mitochondria (e.g., mitochondrial ribosomal proteins like MRPL20, MRPS15). expression correlates cellular metabolic state can confound biological comparisons. Note MT-prefixed genes (encoded mitochondrial genome ) already excluded data preprocessing. 2. Ribosomal protein genes (~190 genes) Ribosomal proteins (RPS RPL gene families) highly ubiquitously expressed across cell types. dominate variance calculations without providing useful biological insight distinguishing developmental disease-related transcriptional changes. 3. text: Normalisation one critical steps single cell analysis. Unlike bulk RNA-seq, samples similar total counts, single cells can vary orders magnitude total UMI counts due differences cell size, RNA content, capture efficiency. SCTransform (Hafemeister & Satija, 2019) uses regularised negative binomial regression normalise UMI count data. approach: Models relationship observed counts sequencing depth gene using negative binomial distribution Computes Pearson residuals represent deviation expected expression given sequencing depth Identifies genes high biological variability (variable features) drive downstream analyses key insight highly expressed genes show variance simply due sampling effects. SCTransform accounts modelling mean-variance relationship, allowing fair comparison across genes different expression levels. vst.flavor = "v2" option uses improved algorithm (Choudhary & Satija, 2022) : Uses geometric mean library size reference (robust) Implements improved regularisation better handling outliers Provides stable results large datasets SCTransform automatically identifies highly variable genes. title: Module 4: Differential Expression Analysis
text: critical pitfall single cell differential expression analysis pseudoreplication: treating cells independent biological replicates . Cells sample share technical biological variation violates independence assumption statistical tests. Consider analogy: want compare heights two populations, measuring person multiple times increase sample size. Similarly, capturing 5,000 cells one individual give us 5,000 independent observations individual’s biology. Many single cell DE methods (Wilcoxon test, t-test, MAST) operate cell level treat cell independent replicate. approaches: Inflate Type error rates (false positives) dramatically Produce artificially small p-values reflect true significance Confound biological technical variation generalise findings beyond specific samples analysed solution pseudobulk analysis: aggregating counts across cells within sample create sample-level expression estimates, applying well-established bulk RNA-seq methods. approach: Correctly identifies biological replicate (sample/individual) Properly controls false discovery rates Accounts sample--sample variation Produces results generalise population

title: Module 7: Cell-specific Co-expression Networks (NeighbourNet)
text: core workflow : resolve target transcription-factor lists; scale selected genes compute PCA; build k-nearest-neighbour graph PC space; set local regressions TFs target genes; run per-cell network regression; aggregate cell-specific networks meta-networks. slowest chunk module, cache Seurat object immediately build.meta.network(). expensive output now lives seu@misc$NNet.mod. useful piece module meta.network$pcs: one row per cell one column per meta-network. can read like network-space embedding, cells close together similar co-expression programs.
code:
nnet_cache <- file.path(     results_dir,     sprintf("07_seu_nnet_%02dtargets.rds", n_targets) )  if (file.exists(nnet_cache)) {     seu <- readRDS(nnet_cache)     message("Loaded cached NeighbourNet object from ", nnet_cache) } else {     # NeighbourNet 1.0.0's select.gene() currently references a hard-coded     # object name internally, so we reproduce the small filtering step here.     select_nnet_genes <- function(seurat_obj, targets, min.cells = 10) {         gene_list <- NeighbourNet::gene.list         genes_all <- rownames(seurat_obj)         counts <- SeuratObject::LayerData(seurat_obj, layer = "counts")         n_cell_expressed <- Matrix::rowSums(counts[genes_all, , drop = FALSE] > 0)         genes_kept <- genes_all[n_cell_expressed > min.cells]          tfs <- intersect(genes_kept, unique(gene_list$tfs))         targets <- intersect(genes_kept, intersect(gene_list$targets, targets))          list(             tfs = tfs,             targets = targets,             bgs = character(0),             genes = unique(c(tfs, targets))         )     }      genes <- select_nnet_genes(seu, targets = top_targets, min.cells = 10)      cat("Predictor TFs:", length(genes$tfs), "
")     cat("Target genes: ", length(genes$targets), "
")     cat("Total genes:  ", length(genes$genes), "
")      if (length(genes$targets) < 5) {         warning("Fewer than five target genes survived filtering; ",                 "the network plots may be sparse.")     }     if (length(genes$genes) < 3) {         stop("Too few genes survived NeighbourNet filtering.")     }      npcs <- min(50, length(genes$genes) - 1, ncol(seu) - 1)     knn <- min(30, ncol(seu) - 1)      seu <- prepare.seurat(seu, genes = genes$genes, npcs = npcs)     seu <- prepare.graph(seu, knn = knn)     seu <- prepare.reg(seu,                        predictors = genes$tfs,                        responses  = genes$targets)     seu <- run.nn.reg(seu,                       responses = genes$targets,                       return.p.val = TRUE)     seu <- build.meta.network(seu, n.net = n_meta_networks)      seu@misc$Module7 <- list(         feature_ranking = rank_tbl,         top_targets = top_targets,         n_targets = n_targets,         n_meta_networks = n_meta_networks     )      saveRDS(seu, nnet_cache) } nnet_mod <- Seurat::Misc(seu, "NNet.mod") names(nnet_mod) names(nnet_mod$meta.network) dim(nnet_mod$meta.network$pcs) dim(nnet_mod$meta.network$meta.network)

code: safe_cor <- function(x, y) {     sx <- stats::sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)     sy <- stats::sd(y, na.rm = TRUE)     if (is.na(sx) || is.na(sy) || sx == 0 || sy == 0) {         return(NA_real_)     }     stats::cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman") }  cor_tbl <- tibble(     meta_network = seq_len(ncol(meta_pcs)),     spearman_cor = apply(meta_pcs, 2, safe_cor, y = seu$pt_phi_score) ) |>     mutate(abs_cor = abs(spearman_cor)) |>     arrange(desc(abs_cor))  cor_tbl  maturation_idx <- cor_tbl$meta_network[1] cat("Meta-network most associated with maturation:", maturation_idx, "\n")

text: Figure 3C paper shows weighted adjacency matrices behind first two meta-networks. heatmap TF--target view meta-network: bright tiles mark TF-target pairs strong aggregated co-expression recurrent network pattern. workshop run keeps 10 requested target genes, five survive NeighbourNet’s target-prior expression filters data, show retained targets top 10 TFs meta-network.
code: plot_adjacency <- function(i, n_tf = 10, n_target = 10) {     mat <- Seurat::Misc(seu, "NNet.mod")$meta.network$meta.network[, , i]      target_score <- Matrix::rowSums(abs(mat))     tf_score <- Matrix::colSums(abs(mat))      targets <- names(sort(target_score, decreasing = TRUE))[         seq_len(min(n_target, length(target_score)))     ]     tfs <- names(sort(tf_score, decreasing = TRUE))[         seq_len(min(n_tf, length(tf_score)))     ]      plot_mat <- t(mat[targets, tfs, drop = FALSE])      if (nrow(plot_mat) > 1) {         plot_mat <- plot_mat[hclust(dist(plot_mat))$order, , drop = FALSE]     }     if (ncol(plot_mat) > 1) {         plot_mat <- plot_mat[, hclust(dist(t(plot_mat)))$order, drop = FALSE]     }      adj_df <- as.data.frame(as.table(plot_mat))     colnames(adj_df) <- c("TF", "Target", "weight")      ggplot(adj_df, aes(Target, TF, fill = weight)) +         geom_tile(colour = "white", linewidth = 0.2) +         scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#B2182B") +         labs(title = paste("Meta-network", i, "weighted adjacency"),              x = "Target gene", y = "TF", fill = "Weight") +         theme_bw(base_size = 11) +         theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) }  plot_adjacency(1) | plot_adjacency(2)

code: central_genes <- select.central.genes(     seu,     n.net = min(2, n_meta_networks),     n.per.component = 4,     k = 2 ) seu <- prepare.visualise(seu, central.genes = central_genes, n.clu = 4)  edge_cutoff <- function(p_mat) {     mean(apply(p_mat, 1, max, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE) }  plot_meta_network <- function(i) {     meta_p <- Seurat::Misc(seu, "NNet.mod")$meta.network$p.val[, , i]     visualise.network(         seu,         i = i,         meta.network = TRUE,         cutoff = edge_cutoff(meta_p),         radius = c(0.4, 0.7, 0.85, 1),         pie.radius = 0.04,         text.size = 4     ) +         labs(title = paste("Meta-network", i)) }  plot_meta_network(1) | plot_meta_network(2)
